analysis.one_liner: Lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission warn the public about dangerous products without first getting manufacturer sign-off.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2023, received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike the part of consumer product safety law that stops the Consumer Product Safety Commission from publicly disclosing information that identifies the maker of a hazardous product unless the agency first verifies the information is accurate and fair to release. Under current law, the manufacturer must also get a chance to comment and can sue in federal court to block a disclosure. Removing those requirements would let the agency warn shoppers about dangerous products faster and name names, but with fewer safeguards for companies that might be wrongly or prematurely accused.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would learn sooner and in more detail when a specific company's product has been linked to injuries or hazards. The CPSC itself would also gain flexibility: today it must negotiate with a manufacturer, and often stays silent for months or years while a hazard investigation plays out, before naming the product publicly. Parents shopping for cribs, toys, and other goods would see the agency's safety concerns in real time rather than after a private back-and-forth with the company.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the section of the Consumer Product Safety Act that prohibits the CPSC from disclosing information identifying a manufacturer unless the agency first takes reasonable steps to ensure the information is accurate and that disclosure is fair in the circumstances and serves the agency's purposes.

Removes the requirement that the CPSC give the manufacturer an opportunity to comment on the accuracy of the information before it is disclosed, and strips the manufacturer's ability to file a federal lawsuit to block a disclosure.

For ordinary people, the practical effect is faster, more specific public warnings: instead of a vague hazard notice that avoids naming the maker while negotiations drag on, the agency could put out what it knows, including the company's identity, when it knows it.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer product manufacturers, who would lose the legally guaranteed pre-disclosure process and the ability to keep the agency's investigation confidential while disputes over accuracy are resolved. Under the bill, a company could see its name attached to a hazard allegation before it has had any chance to correct errors, and without a court option to stop the release. Companies would also face faster reputational damage from preliminary findings that later turn out to be incomplete.

drawbacks.text: The bill strikes not only the disclosure restrictions but also the accuracy safeguards built into them: the requirements that the CPSC take reasonable steps to verify information, that it offer the manufacturer a chance to comment before release, and that the manufacturer be able to go to federal court to block a disclosure. Without those checks, the agency could publish an allegation identifying a company before the facts are confirmed, and an innocent or partially at-fault company would have no way to correct the record or stop the release in time.

Premature public naming of a product can impose large, irreversible costs on a manufacturer even if the underlying concern is later resolved, and companies that fear immediate public exposure may become less willing to cooperate candidly with agency investigations, which could slow down hazard identification overall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real: faster, more specific warnings about hazardous products, ending a process that can keep safety concerns quiet for long stretches while the agency and a company negotiate. The cost is the loss of the procedural protections companies currently have against inaccurate or premature disclosures, which is an honest trade-off rather than a flaw unique to this bill's design — the same balance exists in every public-health disclosure regime. The larger weakness here was political: the bill drew no cosponsors and no committee action, so the trade-off was never publicly tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it quietly died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on March 16, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No cosponsors signed on in either chamber.

The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill was never brought to the Senate floor. That is the entire recorded history of the bill, which expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer product manufacturers came out ahead: the existing restrictions on CPSC disclosures — including the pre-release comment process and the right to sue — remain in force, so the agency still cannot publicly name a company's product over its objection without first meeting the accuracy and fairness requirements.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the disclosure restrictions from the Consumer Product Safety Act; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 16, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 22 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no cosponsors and no votes, so the partisan shape was never tested; the bill simply never moved beyond its Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: Because the bill died, manufacturers keep the legal process that requires the CPSC to verify accuracy, hear their comments, and face potential litigation before publicly tying a hazard to their product. Their interest in keeping that confidentiality runs against consumers' interest in fast, specific warnings about dangerous goods.

The agency keeps the legal constraints it has chafed under: it still must clear the accuracy, fairness, and negotiation requirements of section 6(b) before disclosing information that identifies a manufacturer, limiting how quickly it can warn the public.
